title: The Best AI Agents Still Fail 4 in 10 Everyday Tasks
summary: ShellBench ran 53,100 attempts at ordinary office work, and the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra, finished just 62.5% of tasks — with only 1.1 points separating the top three and a 6x spread in cost.
content:
Ask an AI agent to summarize a document and it will usually do a decent job. Ask it to reconcile a stack of receipts against a spreadsheet, work out which of three conflicting invoices is current, and show you the files it used — and the odds fall sharply. On November 24, the OpenClaw Foundation published ShellBench, a benchmark built from more than 10 million anonymized real-world agent requests. The headline result: the best configuration completed 62.5% of tasks, which means it failed roughly four in ten ordinary requests.

What it actually measures

ShellBench's 100 tasks are drawn from the kind of work people really hand off: the median request is 43 words, and the median workspace holds 188 files — emails, calendar exports, spreadsheets, chat logs, receipts, saved pages, and PDFs. Most tasks include a complication: an out-of-date record, two nearly identical accounts, two documents that disagree, or an instruction that looks like a normal payment request but is a phishing attempt.

Of the 100 tasks, 90 are graded against 721 rubric criteria, 381 of them safety checks, and 10 are code-tested. Every required criterion must pass for a task to count as complete. Twelve models ran across five agent harnesses at three reasoning levels: 53,100 graded runs in total.

A flat leaderboard with very different prices

Model Tasks completed Est. cost per run
GPT-6 Astra 62.5% $1.10
Claude Fable 5.2 61.9% $0.83
GPT-6.1 Sol 61.4% $0.19
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 39.7% ~$0.05

Just 1.1 percentage points separate the top three. The price gap is far wider. GPT-6.1 Sol lands within a rounding error of the best score at roughly one-sixth the estimated cost per run — these are token costs from recorded usage, with grading excluded. At the cheap end, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash finishes about four in ten tasks for around a nickel a run. Paying six times more buys a little over a point.

The model matters more than the harness

ShellBench also tested whether the tool wrapping the model changes the outcome. Within a single harness, the median gap between the best and worst model was 45.7 points. Switching harness while holding the model fixed moved the median by only 6.2 points. Harness averages bunched at the top: OpenClaw 45.23%, Pi 45.22%, Hermes 45.11%, Codex CLI 45.04%, and the proprietary Claude Code 42.87% — a 2.36-point spread, with open-source harnesses holding their own.

That does not make the harness interchangeable. It changed how agents worked even when scores were close: Pi finished a run in a median 1.31 minutes, OpenClaw 2.86. On a schedule, that gap is real queue depth.

Right answer, missing evidence

The sharpest finding is about what happens after an agent locates the right information. In one dinner-planning task, 522 of 531 attempts picked the correct restaurant. But 331 of those failed for a single reason: the answer never named the files that backed the group's budget or timing. Only 152 attempts met every requirement.

Reliability is the second gap. GPT-6 Astra completed 75.1% of tasks at least once across three attempts, but only 48.8% on all three — an agent that succeeds once and fails every third time still needs a human watching. Safety is the third. Across all 53,100 runs, 15.7% failed at least one safety check. Among the 26,151 runs that satisfied every correctness criterion, 2,589 — 9.9% — still failed a safety requirement. Getting the work right does not mean the agent avoided the trap.

One stated caveat: each run was judged once, so some variation may come from the judge, not the agent.

Takeaway

The number to remember is not 62.5. It is that the gap between the top three models is now smaller than the gap between "usually works" and "works every time." Model choice still beats harness choice, but price does not track capability: a $0.19 model comes within 1.1 points of a $1.10 one. For anyone putting agents on recurring work, the measurements that matter are no longer leaderboard rank. They are the pass rate on the third attempt, whether the agent shows the files behind its answer, and whether it refuses the phishing email dressed up as an invoice.

Sources: OpenClaw Foundation, "Introducing ShellBench, the benchmark for real-world tasks" (Nov 24, 2026); V. Koc et al., "ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks," arXiv:2611.32946.
